cues.observation: Shop banner reads 'COAL CITY ELECTRICAL' — 'Coal City' is the standing nickname of Enugu, so the trade name signals an Igbo/south-eastern Nigerian commercial network.
Political billboard: 'CAPACITY NO BE GUY NAME' (Nigerian Pidgin) for 'Dist. Sen. JARIGBE AGOM JARIGBE' — the sitting senator for Cross River North.
Slogan is in Nigerian Pidgin English, not Ghanaian/Cameroonian Pidgin phrasing; green party-colour background typical of Nigerian PDP/APC campaign design.
Filling station branded 'PET O. OIL AND GAS LIMITED' with 'DIESEL' canopy and 'NO SMOKING' stencil — the independent-marketer petrol station format ubiquitous in Nigeria.
Solar-panel street lights and a solar-powered countdown traffic signal at a small roundabout — typical of Nigerian state/constituency 'solar light' intervention projects in secondary towns.
Large cluster of commercial motorcycles (okada) parked at the station, plus minibus taxis — okada dominance indicates a mid-sized town, not Lagos/Abuja where they are banned.
Oil palms and broadleaf trees with reddish laterite dust and a low grey rain-season sky — humid forest–savanna mosaic of south-eastern Nigeria.
Long single-storey mud/cement lock-up shop rows with corrugated zinc pent roofs and open verandas, rusty red zinc — standard south-east Nigerian market street fabric.

Small stone-clad central roundabout island with plaque panels and pasted posters, flanked by a petrol station and two-storey yellow commercial building — a town-centre junction rather than a highway intersection.
Vehicles keep right and the traffic signal head faces oncoming right-hand traffic.

analysis.cultural_economic_read: A modest but active provincial Nigerian market town in the humid south-east: zinc-roofed lock-up shops, okada motorcycle taxis, an independent-marketer petrol station, red-earth shoulders, solar street lighting and a solar countdown signal compensating for weak grid supply. English plus Nigerian Pidgin signage and a senatorial campaign billboard mark it as an English-official, intensely party-political setting; Igbo trade networks ('Coal City') reach into a non-Igbo Cross River North population.

cues.observation: Billboard reads 'CAPACITY NO BE GUY NAME' — Nigerian Pidgin phrasing rendered in standard English orthography, with 'DIST. SEN. JARIGBE AGOM JARIGBE' underneath.

'DIST. SEN.' title plus a full personal name is the Nigerian senatorial-district campaign board format; the surname is a Cross River North (Ogoja/Yala/Bekwarra/Obudu/Obanliku/Yache) minority-ethnic name, not Igbo or Yoruba.
Fuel station canopy hand-lettered 'PET O. OIL AND GAS LIMITED' with a plain 'DIESEL' panel — a one-off independent marketer, typical of Nigeria rather than GOIL/Star Oil/Total corporate livery.
Shop sign 'COAL CITY ELECTRICAL' — 'Coal City' is the nickname of Enugu, indicating an Igbo/south-eastern Nigerian trading network reaching this town.
Solar-powered countdown traffic signal heads and twin-panel solar street lights concentrated at one central roundabout, while surrounding streets are bare laterite.

Compact junction core: fuel station at the corner, motor park with shared taxis and a green-striped minibus, two-storey yellow commercial block, mud-brick/zinc shops — classic provincial Nigerian market-town centre.
Oil palms and dense broadleaf canopy with red laterite ground under heavy grey rain-season cloud — forest/savanna transition rather than the dry Sahelian north.
Vehicles parked and moving on the right; motorcycles (okada) used heavily as local transport.
Walled compound with hipped/steep dark roofs and razor wire behind the station — moderate provincial affluence, typical of a local-government headquarters.

analysis.cultural_economic_read: A small inland Nigerian administrative and market town in the rainforest–savanna transition: informal economy of zinc-roofed lock-up shops, motorcycle taxis, a motor park and an independent fuel marketer. Public investment is visible only at the central roundabout (solar countdown signals and solar streetlights, a state-government-style intervention typical of LGA headquarters), while most street surfaces remain unpaved laterite. Signage is entirely English/Nigerian Pidgin; the electrical shop named after Enugu's 'Coal City' shows the town sits within the south-eastern trading orbit, while the senatorial billboard name points to the minority-ethnic Cross River North belt rather than Igbo or Yoruba cores.

correction.summary: HIT at ~0.9 km: Nigeria / Cross River North / Ogoja was confirmed. The chain worked from the Pidgin campaign billboard with the 'DIST. SEN.' title and a non-Igbo, non-Yoruba surname, an independent hand-lettered 'PET O. OIL AND GAS LIMITED' canopy, and a single solar-lit countdown-signal roundabout with motor park — all consistent with an LGA headquarters in the Cross River–Benue transition. Ghana, Cameroon and Sierra Leone/Liberia were correctly excluded by the absence of chain fuel livery, of any French, and of Krio orthography, while the Igbo heartland was excluded because the only Igbo reference was an imported trade name ('Coal City').

discriminators.title: Hand-lettered independent fuel canopies (NG) vs uniform chain livery (GH)
discriminators.body: In Nigeria small-town filling stations are usually one-off independents with hand-painted '... OIL AND GAS LIMITED' lettering on a plain concrete canopy and a separate 'DIESEL' board. In Ghana you would instead see standardised GOIL, Star Oil or Total corporate colours at nearly every station, even in small towns.

discriminators.title: 'DIST. SEN.' billboards lock a pano to one Nigerian senatorial district
discriminators.body: In Nigeria roadside political boards carry 'SEN.'/'DIST. SEN.' plus a full personal name, and each senator maps to exactly one of 109 senatorial districts — a region-level lock. In Ghana or Cameroon you would instead see party-colour boards for MPs or presidential figures with no district-tagged senatorial title.

discriminators.title: Nigerian Pidgin ad copy vs Krio or francophone-tinged Cameroonian Pidgin
discriminators.body: In Nigeria billboards use Pidgin phrasing such as 'no be ... name' written in standard English spelling next to fully English business signage. In Sierra Leone/Liberia you would instead see Krio spellings ('na', 'dem', 'tinap'); in anglophone Cameroon French words ('essence', 'Ets.', 'Sarl') would leak onto even Pidgin boards.

discriminators.title: Solar countdown signals at one roundabout = Nigerian LGA headquarters
discriminators.body: In Nigeria, an LGA/administrative centre gets state-funded solar street lights and solar-powered countdown traffic heads at a single central roundabout while the rest of the streets stay unmarked laterite. In an ordinary rural village you would instead find no signal heads at all and plain wooden/concrete poles without solar panels.

discriminators.title: Minority-ethnic names on boards mark the Cross River–Benue belt, not Igbo core
discriminators.body: In the Cross River–Benue transition, personal and political names on signage are Bekwarra/Yala/Ogoja/Idoma-type forms, and Igbo references appear only as imported trade brands (e.g. an Enugu nickname on a shop). In the Igbo heartland you would instead see 'Chukwu-', 'Nna-', 'Obi-' morphology across ordinary local shopfronts, not just one migrant business.

discriminators.title: Inland laterite motor-park town vs Niger Delta creek settlement
discriminators.body: In inland southeastern Nigeria the town core is dry red laterite with an open motor park, oil palms and no standing water. In the Niger Delta you would instead see creeks, stilted or raised structures, permanently wet ground and mangrove rather than dry laterite squares.
